'''Thomas Vogt'''  (born 1958) is a German [[chemist]] and [[Materials science|material scientist]]. He is an Educational Foundation Distinguished Professor in the Department of [[Chemistry]] and [[Biochemistry]] at the [[University of South Carolina]].<ref name =aaa>{{Cite web|url=https://sc.edu/study/colleges_schools/chemistry_and_biochemistry/our_people/directory/vogt_thomas.php|title=Thomas Vogt - Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry &#124; University of South Carolina|website=sc.edu}}</ref>

Vogt is most known for his work in [[structural chemistry]], [[chemical synthesis]], and structure-property [[correlation]]s of metal oxides based on [[diffraction]] techniques using [[electron]]s, [[x-ray]]s, and [[neutron]]s.<ref name=ggg>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=TV5fyfgAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Thomas Vogt|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref> He has authored and co-authored over 300 peer-reviewed journal articles and several books such as ''Solid State Materials Chemistry'' and ''Modelling Nanoscale Imaging in Electron Microscopy''. He is the recipient of the 1996 R&D 100 award from ''R&D Magazine'', the 2002 Design and Engineering Award of [[Popular Mechanics]], the 2018 Carolina Trustee Professorship Award, and the 2019 USC Educational Foundation Award in Science, Mathematics and Engineering.<ref name=usc>{{Cite web|url=https://sc.edu/about/offices_and_divisions/provost/about/honorsandawards/provost_awards/awardwinners.php|title=Previous Award Winners - Office of the Provost &#124; University of South Carolina|website=sc.edu}}</ref>

Vogt is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org}}</ref> the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/listing|title=Elected Fellows &#124; American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)}}</ref> the Neutron Scattering Society of America,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://neutronscattering.org/prizes/nssa-fellows/|title=NSSA Fellows|website=neutronscattering.org}}</ref> as well as of the [[Institute of Advanced Study (Durham)|Institute of Advanced Study at Durham University]]<ref name=ddd>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iasdurham.org/people/former-fellows/structure-fellows/professor-thomas-vogt/|title=Professor Thomas Vogt &#124; IAS Durham}}</ref> and was a Founding Member of the editorial board for ''[[Physical Review Applied]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://journals.aps.org/prapplied/edannounce/PhysRevApplied.1.010001|title=Editorial: Troy Shinbrot Introduces Physical Review Applied|date=February 25, 2014|website=Physical Review Applied}}</ref>

==Education==
Vogt earned a Diploma in Chemistry in 1985, followed by a PhD in 1987, both from the [[University of Tübingen]].<ref name=ddd/>

==Career==
After working at a European and US national laboratory ([[Institut Laue–Langevin|Institute Laue Langevin]] and [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]), Vogt began an academic career at the Department of [[Philosophy]] at the [[University of South Carolina]]. He teaches The History and [[Philosophy of chemistry|Philosophy of Chemistry]] in the South Carolina Honors College. Later he became a professor in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at the University of South Carolina, where he has been the Educational Foundation Distinguished Professor since 2010.<ref name=aaa/>

From 2005 to 2023, Vogt served as Director of the NanoCenter at the University of South Carolina<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wistv.com/story/3653385/usc-names-scientist-to-lead-nanocenter|title=USC names scientist to lead NanoCenter|date=July 28, 2005|website=www.wistv.com}}</ref> and was Associate Vice President for Research from 2011 to 2013, and a member on the Board of Directors of the USC Research Foundation from 2008 to 2012. He was the co-chair of the Search Committee for [[Provost (education)|Provost]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sc.edu/study/colleges_schools/chemistry_and_biochemistry/about/news/2020/mar_31_vogt_provost_search_committee.php|title=Congratulations Thomas Vogt - Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry &#124; University of South Carolina|website=www.sc.edu}}</ref> and Chief Academic Officer in 2019 and later a Pearce Faculty Fellow in the South Carolina Honors College from 2020 to 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sc.edu/study/colleges_schools/honors_college/about/our_people/faculty_fellows/index.php|title=Pearce Faculty Fellows - South Carolina Honors College &#124; University of South Carolina|website=sc.edu}}</ref>

Before joining the University of South Carolina, Vogt worked as a Scientist at the Institute Laue-Langevin, France until 1992, then joined Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) as an Associate Physicist, promoted to Physicist in 1995,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/04/08/IHT-american-topics-short-takes.html|title=AMERICAN TOPICS: Short Takes|work=The New York Times |date=8 April 1996 }}</ref> and by 2000, he led the Powder Diffraction Group in BNL's Physics Department. From 2003 to 2005, he held various roles at BNL, including Head of Materials Synthesis and Characterization Group, Cluster Leader of Materials Synthesis in the Center for Functional Nanomaterials (CFN), and Technical Coordinator for scientific equipment in the CFN building project. Moreover, he led three startups,  Nanosource, LUMINOF and Sens4 as the Chief Technology Officer. He is a limited partner of TEXXMO mobile solutions, a wearable computer company and IOT button manufacturer.<ref name=aaa/>

==Research==
Vogt has conducted basic research using neutron, x-ray, and [[electron diffraction]] techniques to study structure-property relationships in materials, while also exploring philosophical and ethical implications of science and technology, particularly concerning the emergence of the [[periodic table]] of chemical elements.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The value of vague ideas in the development of the periodic system of chemical elements|first=Thomas|last=Vogt|date=December 1, 2021|journal=Synthese|volume=199|issue=3|pages=10587–10614|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/s11229-021-03260-y}}</ref> He holds 11 US patents such as the development of multidimensional integrated detection and analysis system (MIDAS)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8236569B2/en|title=Multi-dimensional integrated detection and analysis system (MIDAS) based on microcantilvers}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8252598B2/en|title=Method of sensing chemical and bio-molecular analytes and sensing system using a microcantilever}}</ref> and neutron scintillating materials.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8475681B2/en|title=Neutron scintillating materials}}</ref>

===Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)===
Vogt investigated complex material structures using aberration-corrected [[scanning transmission electron microscopy]] (STEM).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/559257|title=Keck Futures Initiative awards $1 million for 13 research projects|website=EurekAlert!}}</ref> He helped develop new image simulation and modeling methodologies, such as super-resolution techniques, specialized de-noising methods, mathematical and statistical learning theories, and applications of compressed sensing, outlined in the book  ''Modelling Nanoscale Imaging in Electron Microscopy''. In a review for ''Physics Today'', Les J. Allen commented, "In six chapters, the editors tackle the ambitious challenge of bridging the gap between high-level applied mathematics and experimental electron microscopy. They have met the challenge admirably... That work is also applicable to the new generation of x-ray free-electron lasers, which have similar prospective applications, and illustrates nicely the importance of applied mathematics in the physical sciences."<ref>{{Cite journal|title=''Modeling Nanoscale Imaging in Electron Microscopy''|first=Les J.|last=Allen|date=May 1, 2012|journal=Physics Today|volume=65|issue=5|pages=54–55|doi=10.1063/pt.3.1562|bibcode=2012PhT....65e..54A }}</ref>

Vogt and collaborators using STEM imaging with spherical aberration imaged the M1 phase, a MoVNbTe oxide partial oxidation catalyst, highlighting its potential applications in complex materials structure analysis.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ange.200705700|title=Direct Imaging of the MoVTeNbO M1 Phase Using An Aberration-Corrected High-Resolution Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope|first1=William D.|last1=Pyrz|first2=Douglas A.|last2=Blom|first3=Thomas|last3=Vogt|first4=Douglas J.|last4=Buttrey|date=March 31, 2008|journal=Angewandte Chemie|volume=120|issue=15|pages=2830–2833|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1002/ange.200705700|bibcode=2008AngCh.120.2830P |url-access=subscription}}</ref> He also used the annular dark-field STEM to analyze nanoscale domains of complex oxide phases in disordered solids development.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=ADF-STEM Imaging of Nascent Phases and Extended Disorder Within the Mo–V–Nb–Te–O Catalyst System|first1=T.|last1=Vogt|first2=D. A.|last2=Blom|first3=L.|last3=Jones|first4=D. J.|last4=Buttrey|date=October 1, 2016|journal=Topics in Catalysis|volume=59|issue=17|pages=1489–1495|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/s11244-016-0665-0}}</ref> Furthermore, he and Douglas Blom employed parallel computing to analyze compositional disorder in a Mo, V-oxide bronze, highlighting discrepancies between experimental and simulated V content along metal-oxygen atomic columns, validated by HAADF-STEM imaging.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Probing Compositional Order in Atomic Columns: STEM Simulations Beyond the Virtual Crystal Approximation|date=2020 |doi=10.1017/S1431927619015198 |last1=Blom |first1=Douglas A. |last2=Vogt |first2=Thomas |journal=Microscopy and Microanalysis |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=46–52 |pmid=31839023 |bibcode=2020MiMic..26...46B }}</ref>

===Crystallography===
Vogt used high-resolution neutron  diffraction techniques to investigate structural changes in molecules. Alongside Andrew N. Fitch and Jeremy K. Cockcroft, he revealed the low-temperature crystal structure of Rhenium heptafluoride (ReF7), confirming its molecular configuration as a distorted pentagonal bipyramid with Cs (m) symmetry.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.263.5151.1265|title=Crystal and Molecular Structures of Rhenium Heptafluoride|first1=T.|last1=Vogt|first2=A. N.|last2=Fitch|first3=J. K.|last3=Cockcroft|date=March 4, 1994|journal=Science|volume=263|issue=5151|pages=1265–1267|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1126/science.263.5151.1265|pmid=17817431 |bibcode=1994Sci...263.1265V |url-access=subscription}}</ref> In another joint study published in ''Science'', he observed negative thermal expansion in [[Zirconium tungstate|ZrW{{sub|2}}O{{sub|8}}]], using diffraction to analyze its cubic structure.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.272.5258.90|title=Negative Thermal Expansion from 0.3 to 1050 Kelvin in ZrW 2 O 8|first1=T. A.|last1=Mary|first2=J. S. O.|last2=Evans|first3=T.|last3=Vogt|first4=A. W.|last4=Sleight|date=April 5, 1996|journal=Science|volume=272|issue=5258|pages=90–92|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1126/science.272.5258.90|bibcode=1996Sci...272...90M |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Using high-resolution neutron powder diffraction, Czjzek and Vogt located the hydrogen positions in zeolite Y.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/j100183a009|title=Direct determination of proton positions in D-Y and H-Y zeolite samples by neutron powder diffraction|first1=Mirjam|last1=Czjzek|first2=Herve|last2=Jobic|first3=Andrew N.|last3=Fitch|first4=Thomas|last4=Vogt|date=February 5, 1992|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|volume=96|issue=4|pages=1535–1540|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/j100183a009|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Subsequently, with Yongjae Lee, he examined structural changes in zeolites at high pressures, showing a pronounced rearrangement of non-framework metal ions and pressure-induced hydration/superhydration.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature01265|title=Non-framework cation migration and irreversible pressure-induced hydration in a zeolite|first1=Yongjae|last1=Lee|first2=Thomas|last2=Vogt|first3=Joseph A.|last3=Hriljac|first4=John B.|last4=Parise|first5=Jonathan C.|last5=Hanson|first6=Sun Jin|last6=Kim|date=December 5, 2002|journal=Nature|volume=420|issue=6915|pages=485–489|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/nature01265|pmid=12466838 |bibcode=2002Natur.420..485L |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Solid-state chemistry===
Vogt's work on [[solid-state chemistry]] has focused on the temperature and pressure-dependent structural arrangements of materials. In 2021, he co-authored a textbook ''Solid State Materials Chemistry'' with Patrick M. Woodward, Pavel Karen and John S.O. Evans, covering structure, defects, bonding, and properties of solid state materials. He reported a spin ordering transition in oxygen-deficient YBaCo{{sub|2}}O{{sub|5}}, accompanied by structural changes and spin state alterations, marking the first observation of this phenomenon induced by long-range orbital and charge ordering.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.2969|title=Low to High Spin-State Transition Induced by Charge Ordering in Antiferromagnetic YBaCo<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> |pmid=11018988 |last1=Vogt |first1=T. |last2=Woodward |first2=P. M. |last3=Karen |first3=P. |last4=Hunter |first4=B. A. |last5=Henning |first5=P. |last6=Moodenbaugh |first6=A. R. |hdl=10852/59525 |hdl-access=free |date=March 27, 2000|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=84|issue=13|pages=2969–2972|via=APS|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.2969}}</ref> He collaborated on the characterization of a new solid electrolyte, Bi{{sub|2}}La{{sub|8}}[(GeO{{sub|4}}){{sub|6}}]O{{sub|3}}, identifying oxide ion interstitials as key to its ionic conductivity using advanced dark field electron microscopy.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adfm.201605625|title=New Apatite-Type Oxide Ion Conductor, Bi 2 La 8 [(GeO 4 ) 6 ]O 3: Structure, Properties, and Direct Imaging of Low-Level Interstitial Oxygen Atoms Using Aberration-Corrected Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy|first1=Matthew L.|last1=Tate|first2=Douglas A.|last2=Blom|first3=Maxim|last3=Avdeev|first4=Helen E. A.|last4=Brand|first5=Garry J.|last5=McIntyre|first6=Thomas|last6=Vogt|first7=Ivana Radosavljevic|last7=Evans|date=February 5, 2017|journal=Advanced Functional Materials|volume=27|issue=8|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1002/adfm.201605625}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US6613213B1/en|title=Method for producing electrodes using microscale or nanoscale materials obtained from hydrogendriven metallurgical reactions}}</ref> Furthermore, he investigated the cubic structure of CaCu{{sub|3}}Ti{{sub|4}}O{{sub|12}}, a material with a large optical conductivity, ruling out ferroelectricity in favor of relaxor-like dynamics responsible for its giant dielectric effect.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1061655|title=Optical Response of High-Dielectric-Constant Perovskite-Related Oxide|first1=C. C.|last1=Homes|first2=T.|last2=Vogt|first3=S. M.|last3=Shapiro|first4=S.|last4=Wakimoto|first5=A. P.|last5=Ramirez|date=July 27, 2001|journal=Science|volume=293|issue=5530|pages=673–676|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1126/science.1061655|pmid=11474105 |bibcode=2001Sci...293..673H |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Giant dielectric constant response in a copper-titanate|first1=A.P|last1=Ramirez|first2=M.A|last2=Subramanian|first3=M|last3=Gardel|first4=G|last4=Blumberg|first5=D|last5=Li|first6=T|last6=Vogt|first7=S.M|last7=Shapiro|date=June 5, 2000|journal=Solid State Communications|volume=115|issue=5|pages=217–220|doi=10.1016/s0038-1098(00)00182-4|bibcode=2000SSCom.115..217R }}</ref>

In a paper published in ''Nature Chemistry'', Vogt and collaborators demonstrated the irreversible insertion and trapping of xenon in Ag-natrolite under moderate conditions, a possible explanation xenon deficiency in terrestrial and Martian atmospheres.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nchem.1997|title=Irreversible xenon insertion into a small-pore zeolite at moderate pressures and temperatures|first1=Donghoon|last1=Seoung|first2=Yongmoon|last2=Lee|first3=Hyunchae|last3=Cynn|first4=Changyong|last4=Park|first5=Kwang-Yong|last5=Choi|first6=Douglas A.|last6=Blom|first7=William J.|last7=Evans|first8=Chi-Chang|last8=Kao|first9=Thomas|last9=Vogt|first10=Yongjae|last10=Lee|date=September 5, 2014|journal=Nature Chemistry|volume=6|issue=9|pages=835–839|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/nchem.1997|pmid=25143221 |bibcode=2014NatCh...6..835S |osti=1158896 }}</ref> He also observed water insertion into kaolinite at 2.7 GPa and 200 °C, shedding light on water release in subduction zones and its effects on seismicity and volcanic activity. Furthermore, his research showcased a pressure-driven metathesis reaction resulting in the formation of a water-free pollucite phase, CsAlSi{{sub|2}}O{{sub|6}}, with potential applications in nuclear waste remediation.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/es504659z|title=Pressure-Induced Metathesis Reaction To Sequester Cs|first1=Junhyuck|last1=Im|first2=Donghoon|last2=Seoung|first3=Seung Yeop|last3=Lee|first4=Douglas A.|last4=Blom|first5=Thomas|last5=Vogt|first6=Chi-Chang|last6=Kao|first7=Yongjae|last7=Lee|date=January 6, 2015|journal=Environmental Science & Technology|volume=49|issue=1|pages=513–519|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/es504659z|pmid=25515673 |bibcode=2015EnST...49..513I |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Vogt and colleagues used advanced laser techniques to observe sub nanosecond structural dynamics of iron, revealing intricate wave patterns during compression and shock decay.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Subnanosecond phase transition dynamics in laser-shocked iron|first1=H.|last1=Hwang|first2=E.|last2=Galtier|first3=H.|last3=Cynn|first4=I.|last4=Eom|first5=S. H.|last5=Chun|first6=Y.|last6=Bang|first7=G. C.|last7=Hwang|first8=J.|last8=Choi|first9=T.|last9=Kim|first10=M.|last10=Kong|first11=S.|last11=Kwon|first12=K.|last12=Kang|first13=H. J.|last13=Lee|first14=C.|last14=Park|first15=J. I.|last15=Lee|first16=Yongmoon|last16=Lee|first17=W.|last17=Yang|first18=S.-H.|last18=Shim|first19=T.|last19=Vogt|first20=Sangsoo|last20=Kim|first21=J.|last21=Park|first22=Sunam|last22=Kim|first23=D.|last23=Nam|first24=J. H.|last24=Lee|first25=H.|last25=Hyun|first26=M.|last26=Kim|first27=T.-Y.|last27=Koo|first28=C.-C.|last28=Kao|first29=T.|last29=Sekine|first30=Yongjae|last30=Lee|date=June 5, 2020|journal=Science Advances|volume=6|issue=23|article-number=eaaz5132 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aaz5132|pmid=32548258|pmc=7274792|bibcode=2020SciA....6.5132H }}</ref> He also examined the structural phase transitions in silicon 2D-nanosheets under high pressure, revealing size and shape-dependent behavior and the formation of 1D nanowires with reduced thermal conductivity.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Pressure-driven phase transitions and reduction of dimensionality in 2D silicon nanosheets|first1=Gil Chan|last1=Hwang|first2=Douglas A.|last2=Blom|first3=Thomas|last3=Vogt|first4=Jaejun|last4=Lee|first5=Heon-Jin|last5=Choi|first6=Sen|last6=Shao|first7=Yanming|last7=Ma|first8=Yongjae|last8=Lee|date=December 21, 2018|journal=Nature Communications|volume=9|issue=1|page=5412|doi=10.1038/s41467-018-07832-4|doi-access=free|pmid=30575737|pmc=6303324|bibcode=2018NatCo...9.5412H }}</ref>

===Phosphor materials for lighting===
Vogt contributed to the development of white phosphors for fluorescent lighting. Together with Sangmoon Park, he developed a family of self-activating and doped UV phosphors for fluorescent white-light production.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8168086B2/en|title=Inorganic luminescent phosphor materials for lighting}}</ref> They also developed up-conversion phosphors emitting shorter-wavelength light in an ordered oxyfluoride compound.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8673180B2/en|title=Up-conversion white light phosphors}}</ref>
